say.text: A 34-year-old man is brought in after a kitchen fire. He has burns over the head and neck, the whole front of the trunk and the perineum.
Roughly what total body surface area is burnt, by the adult rule of nines?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go region by region and give each one its own figure. Which regions carry the 9s, and which the 18s?
That is not right. The head looks like the biggest part of this burn, so it is tempting to give it the larger figure.
In an adult the head and neck is no bigger a share than one arm. Recheck it against the arms, then add again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the belief to replace: the adult head is not the big block of the chart. The legs and trunk are.

say.text: That is not right. It looks as if one region was left out: the perineum is tiny, so it is easy to drop.
It still has its own figure on the adult chart, the smallest of all. Count it in, then add again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the small regions: a tiny region still counts, and the chart reserves a figure for it.

say.text: Yes. Head and neck 9, anterior trunk 18 and perineum 1 gives 28%. Each arm is 9 and each leg 18, and the whole adult chart adds to 100.

choices.label: I know both charts: skip to the final check

say.text: The adult rule of nines: head and neck 9, each arm 9, front of trunk 18, back of trunk 18, each leg 18, perineum 1. That adds to 100.
Use one rule for every region: nines for the head and arms, eighteens for the trunk sides and legs, and a single percent for the perineum.
Now a 2-year-old with scalds over the whole head and both legs.
Which method should you use to estimate the TBSA?

choices.label: Wallace rule of nines, adult values
Palm method, one palm per percent
Lund and Browder chart, scaled by age
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Picture a toddler's body. Its head is proportionally bigger and its legs smaller than an adult's. Which chart accounts for that?
That is not right. The adult chart is the one most people learn first, so it feels safe for any scald.
The rule of nines is built for adults. A child's proportions differ, so age has to come first.

sure_note.text: You were sure the adult chart fits any burn. It does not: age changes the proportions before anything else.

say.text: That is not right. The palm method is for small or patchy burns, a few spots at most.
A scald over the whole head and both legs is extensive, so it needs a chart that also corrects for age.

sure_note.text: You were sure the palm would do. It suits small patches, not whole regions of a child.

say.text: Yes. Lund and Browder corrects each region for age. In a child the head is about 18% and each leg about 14%.
The adult rule of nines overestimates a child's legs and underestimates the head. Lund and Browder corrects for age.
In a child the head is about 18% and each leg about 14%. Use the age-based chart for every region, not only the head and legs.
Toddler: big head, short legs. Adult: small head, long legs. The same burn adds up differently.
Same 2-year-old: the whole head and both whole legs are burnt.
Total TBSA on the child chart?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Do the head first, then one leg, then double the leg. Use the child figures for each, not the adult ones.
That is not right. Those are adult figures for both regions: the head as an adult's and the legs as adults'.
A toddler's head is a bigger share and each leg a smaller share. Redo both regions on the child chart.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the belief to replace: the adult chart is not the default once the stem gives a child's age.

say.text: That is not right. The head looks correct, and then the leg feels right too, so the adult leg figure slipped in.
That mixes two models. Once the head follows the child chart, use the child rule for every region, legs included.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the mix: one age rule applies to every region, not a child head with adult legs.

say.text: Yes. Head about 18% plus two legs at about 14% each gives 46%. The adult chart would have given a different answer.
Count only partial-thickness and full-thickness areas toward TBSA. Simple erythema is not counted.
For small, patchy burns the palm with fingers is about 1%.
Final check. Which set of adult values adds up to 100%?
Total each pair: arms, legs, and the trunk front plus back.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Add each set up, starting with the head and the perineum. Which set makes exactly 100?
That is not right. The head is a big region, so 18 feels like a head figure.
Check the sum: with the head at 18 the set reaches 109, so one region is too large.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the head: in an adult it is not an 18.

say.text: That is not right. The perineum is small, and nine is the figure you remember most.
Check the sum: with the perineum at 9 the set reaches 108, so one region is too large.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the smallest region: it takes the smallest figure on the chart.

say.text: Yes. Head 9, arms 18, trunk 36, legs 36, perineum 1 makes 100%. Run that sum check every time you estimate.
For a child, switch to Lund and Browder, which corrects for age: head about 18% and each leg about 14%.
